strengths: Well-motivated problem and intuitive solution: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of single-LoRA methods and proposes a principled approach to address it through learnable basis decomposition with dynamic composition.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: Multiple complementary metrics (LPIPS, CLIP directional, VLM-based assessment, 2AFC, user study), validation of VLM-human alignment (89.9%), and systematic ablation studies demonstrate thorough experimental methodology.

Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over baselines with clear Pareto frontier advantages (higher edit accuracy while maintaining input consistency). User preferences align with automated metrics.
Thoughtful experimental design: Clear demonstration that results depend on analogy pairs (Fig. 7), separate in-domain/out-of-domain evaluation, justified encoder design choices through ablations.
Clear presentation and reproducibility efforts: Well-written paper with effective visualizations. Implementation details provided; code/data promised for release.
Practical utility: Lightweight approach that works within existing diffusion frameworks without significant computational overhead.
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: The contribution primarily combines existing ideas (Dravid et al. [12] on LoRA basis + standard attention mechanisms). Joint training strategy is the main novelty, which is incremental for a top-tier venue.
Single model evaluation: Only Flux.1-Kontext tested; generalization to other diffusion models (SD 3, DALL-E, etc.) remains unclear, limiting impact claims and practical applicability.

Dataset and evaluation concerns: Training set is small (16K pairs); custom evaluation dataset (540 triplets) constructed by authors with potential bias; filtering process (removing prompts where Flux fails) may systematically favor the method; limited concept categories (only 3).

Lack of theoretical justification: No validation that LoRA spaces support meaningful linear interpolation. Choice of N=32, r=4 not well justified (ablations show N=16, r=4 performs similarly). Softmax normalization empirically validated but not theoretically motivated.

Missing technical analysis: No visualization of what basis LoRAs specialize in; no analysis of learned attention coefficients; missing parameter efficiency and inference cost comparisons; no investigation of failure modes or when linear composition breaks down.

Incomplete comparison to alternatives: No comparison to simply using a larger single LoRA with equivalent parameters. Out-of-domain evaluation uses pre-trained LoRAs to define the distribution—somewhat circular, not truly testing unseen transformation types.

Reproducibility limitations: Custom dataset not publicly available (only promised on 'website'); complex dataset construction process difficult to reproduce; some experimental details (LLM prompts) incomplete; user study is relatively small (33 users, 45 pairs).
Limited scope of baselines: Only 4 baselines; some dated; no evaluation on established benchmarks if available. No exploration of alternative composition strategies beyond softmax weighting.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with quantitative metrics, user studies (33 users), and extensive ablations that thoroughly validate design choices
Novel LoRA basis decomposition approach that achieves strong generalization to unseen visual analogy tasks compared to single-adapter methods
Detailed implementation documentation and thorough appendices (B.1-B.7) including failure case analysis, enhancing reproducibility and transparency
Clear technical soundness: well-motivated method combining CLIP encoder with LoRA basis mixing for flexible visual analogy learning
Fair and extensive baseline comparisons including DIA, PairEdit, RelationAdapter, VisualClose, and EditTransfer with consistent improvements
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes, with explicit acknowledgment of cases where the method struggles
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution reduces to combining existing components (LoRA + CLIP encoder + flow models) with straightforward coefficient computation via Eq. 4
Modest performance gains in many cases: improvements over baselines are often small margins (Table 1, Fig. 5), not representing substantial advances
Dataset and evaluation limitations: custom Unsplash-based dataset with only 90 unseen test tasks across 3 concept categories; construction methodology lacks rigor for diverse generalization claims

Evaluation methodology concerns: heavy reliance on VLM-based metrics (Gemma-3) which may have inherent biases; small user study (33 users, 45 pairs); quantitative differences often show only 2-3 significant figures

Technical clarity issues: the encoder-to-coefficient pipeline (Eqs. 3-4) is convoluted and could be streamlined; the role of projection module P underexplored; 'Mixed LoRA' concept in Section 3.2 takes effort to understand
Insufficient justification for design choices: limited ablation on basis size N (fixed at 32), rank r (fixed at 4), CLIP encoder selection, and other architectural decisions

Demonstrated limitations: explicit failure cases (Fig. S8) and sensitivity to reference pairs (Appendix B.4) indicate practical constraints; generalization remains limited to tasks similar to training distribution
